learn.hook: Every whole number above 1 is built from prime 'bricks' — and there is only ONE way to build it!
points: A prime has exactly two factors: 1 and itself. A composite number has more than two.
Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic: every composite number can be written as a product of primes, and this factorisation is unique apart from the order of the primes.
Find it with a factor tree or by dividing again and again by the smallest prime that fits.
Write repeated primes as powers: 360 = 2³ × 3² × 5.
A number ends in 0 only if both 2 and 5 are among its prime factors. So 6ⁿ = 2ⁿ × 3ⁿ can never end in 0.

example.q: Write 4620 as a product of primes.

learn.reallife: Computer security (like the lock on your UPI app) depends on how hard it is to find the prime factors of huge numbers.

games.title: Match each number to its prime factorisation
Prime brick check
items: Every composite number can be written as a product of primes.
That is exactly what the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic says.
4ⁿ ends in the digit 0 for some natural number n.
4ⁿ = 2²ⁿ has only the prime 2. Ending in 0 needs both 2 and 5.
The prime factorisation of 45 is 3² × 5.
3² × 5 = 9 × 5 = 45, and 3 and 5 are primes.
9 is a prime factor of 81.
9 is a factor of 81 but 9 is not prime. The only prime factor of 81 is 3.
Writing 5 × 3 × 2 instead of 2 × 3 × 5 gives a different prime factorisation.
Uniqueness is 'apart from the order', so both are the same factorisation of 30.
10ⁿ ends in 0 for every natural number n.
10ⁿ = 2ⁿ × 5ⁿ always contains both 2 and 5.

quiz.q: Which is the prime factorisation of 360?
quiz.explain: 360 = 2 × 2 × 2 × 3 × 3 × 5 = 2³ × 3² × 5. Every factor must be prime.
quiz.mistake: Stops at a composite factor like 10 or 15, or miscounts the 2s

quiz.q: Riya's secret number is 2² × 3 × 5² × 7. What is the number?
quiz.explain: Multiply out the powers: 4 × 3 × 25 × 7 = 2100.
quiz.mistake: Uses 5 instead of 5², or 2 instead of 2²

quiz.q: Why can 6ⁿ never end in the digit 0, for any natural number n?
options: Because its only prime factors are 2 and 3, so 5 never appears
quiz.explain: To end in 0 a number needs both 2 and 5 as prime factors. 6ⁿ = 2ⁿ × 3ⁿ has no 5, and by uniqueness it can never get one.
quiz.mistake: Thinks being even is enough to end in 0

quiz.q: How many different prime factors does 2310 have?
quiz.explain: 2310 = 2 × 3 × 5 × 7 × 11, so it has 5 different primes.
quiz.mistake: Stops dividing too early and leaves a composite factor such as 77

quiz.q: For which value of b does bⁿ end in the digit 0 for every natural number n?
quiz.explain: 10 = 2 × 5, so 10ⁿ = 2ⁿ × 5ⁿ always has both 2 and 5. 12 has no 5, while 15 and 25 have no 2.
quiz.mistake: Thinks having just one of the primes 2 or 5 is enough

quiz.q: Which is the prime factorisation of 156?
quiz.mistake: Leaves a composite factor like 26 or 39 in the answer

quiz.q: Arjun's number is 2⁴ × 5³. What is it?
quiz.mistake: Multiplies the base by the power (2 × 4, 5 × 3) instead of repeated multiplication

quiz.q: The theorem says the prime factorisation is 'unique'. What does unique mean here?
options: Only prime numbers can be factorised
The primes must be written from largest to smallest
Every number has a different number of factors
There is only one set of primes, apart from the order they are written in
quiz.explain: However you split a number, you always end with the same primes the same number of times; only the order may change.
quiz.mistake: Confuses 'unique' with a fixed writing order

teach.ask: Gappu flaps in: 'Why is 2 × 2 × 3 the only way to break 12 into primes? Teach me!'
teach.praise: Tweet! Same primes every time, only the order changes. My prime bricks are sorted!
teach.nudge: But what if I write the primes in a different order — is that a new factorisation?

topics.title: HCF and LCM using prime factors

learn.hook: Two bells, three buses or a box of laddoos — HCF and LCM tell you when things meet and how to share fairly!
points: Write each number as a product of primes first.
HCF = product of the SMALLEST power of each prime that is common to all the numbers.
LCM = product of the GREATEST power of every prime that appears in any of the numbers.
For two positive integers a and b: HCF(a, b) × LCM(a, b) = a × b. This rule does not work in general for three numbers.
The HCF always divides the LCM.

example.q: Find the HCF and LCM of 84 and 120, and check the product rule.
steps: Common primes with smallest powers: 2² and 3, so HCF = 12
All primes with greatest powers: 2³, 3, 5, 7, so LCM = 8 × 3 × 5 × 7 = 840

learn.reallife: Traffic lights that turn green together, school bells, or packing sweets into equal boxes for Diwali gifts all use HCF and LCM.

items.text: If HCF = 5 and LCM = 60 for two numbers, their product = ___
HCF of 2³ × 3 and 2² × 3² = ___

quiz.q: What is the HCF of 36 and 60?
quiz.explain: 36 = 2² × 3² and 60 = 2² × 3 × 5. Common primes with smallest powers: 2² × 3 = 12.
quiz.mistake: Picks a smaller common factor, or gives the LCM

quiz.q: What is the LCM of 36 and 60?
quiz.explain: Take every prime with its greatest power: 2² × 3² × 5 = 180.
quiz.mistake: Just multiplies the two numbers (36 × 60 = 2160)

quiz.q: The HCF of two numbers is 9 and their LCM is 270. One number is 45. What is the other?
quiz.explain: HCF × LCM = product of the two numbers, so the other number = 9 × 270 ÷ 45 = 54.
quiz.mistake: Divides LCM by the number without using the HCF (270 ÷ 45 = 6) or guesses a multiple of 9

quiz.q: If HCF(a, b) = 1, then LCM(a, b) is equal to…
quiz.explain: HCF × LCM = a × b. With HCF = 1, LCM = a × b.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the LCM must also be 1

quiz.q: Can two numbers have HCF 16 and LCM 380?
options: Yes, any HCF and LCM are possible
No, because 380 is not a prime
quiz.explain: The HCF must always divide the LCM. 380 ÷ 16 = 23.75, not a whole number, so this is impossible.
quiz.mistake: Does not know that the HCF always divides the LCM

quiz.q: Three temple bells ring every 12, 15 and 20 minutes. They ring together at 8:00 AM. When will they next ring together?
quiz.explain: They meet after LCM(12, 15, 20) = 60 minutes, which is 9:00 AM.
quiz.mistake: Adds the gaps (12 + 15 + 20 = 47 min) or uses the largest gap only

quiz.q: Meena has 96 laddoos and 120 barfis. She packs them in boxes, one kind per box, with the same number in every box and as many as possible per box. How many sweets go in each box?
quiz.explain: The biggest number that divides both 96 and 120 is HCF(96, 120) = 24.
quiz.mistake: Uses the LCM (480) when the problem asks for the greatest equal share

quiz.q: For the three numbers 4, 6 and 8, what is HCF × LCM?
quiz.explain: HCF(4, 6, 8) = 2 and LCM = 24, so HCF × LCM = 48. That is NOT 4 × 6 × 8 = 192, so the product rule is only for two numbers.
quiz.mistake: Assumes HCF × LCM = product of the numbers also works for three numbers

teach.ask: Gappu is puzzled: 'How do I find the HCF and LCM of two numbers using primes?'
teach.praise: Chirp chirp! Smallest common powers for HCF, biggest powers for LCM. I can share my laddoos now!
teach.nudge: Which powers do I pick for the HCF and which for the LCM — the smaller or the bigger ones?

learn.hook: √2 has been hiding as a 'fake fraction' for 2500 years — today you catch it with a proof!
points: A number is irrational if it cannot be written as p/q where p and q are integers and q ≠ 0. Examples: √2, √3, √5, π.
We prove irrationality by contradiction: assume the number is rational, then reach something impossible.
Key fact: if a prime p divides a², then p divides a.
Proof idea for √2: assume √2 = a/b with a, b co-prime. Squaring gives a² = 2b², so 2 divides a. Put a = 2c: then b² = 2c², so 2 divides b too — but a and b had no common factor. Contradiction!
Rational + irrational is irrational, and a non-zero rational × irrational is irrational. But two irrationals can add or multiply to a rational (√2 × √2 = 2).

example.q: Show that 5 + 3√2 is irrational, given that √2 is irrational.
steps: Assume 5 + 3√2 = r, where r is rational
(r − 5)/3 is rational, because rationals are closed under subtraction and division by a non-zero number
That would make √2 rational — a contradiction

learn.reallife: Engineers use √2 for the diagonal of a square tile and π for round wheels — their decimals never end or repeat, so measurements are always rounded.

games.title: Rational or irrational?
items: π

games.title: Put the proof that √5 is irrational in order
items: Assume √5 = a/b, where a and b are co-prime integers
Square both sides: a² = 5b²
So 5 divides a²; hence 5 divides a. Write a = 5c
Then 25c² = 5b², so b² = 5c² and 5 divides b
5 divides both a and b, which contradicts co-prime, so √5 is irrational

quiz.q: Which of these is irrational?
quiz.explain: √12 = 2√3 and √3 is irrational. √16 = 4, 0.75 = 3/4 and 22/7 are all fractions.
quiz.mistake: Thinks 22/7 is irrational because it is close to π

quiz.q: To prove √3 is irrational we assume √3 = a/b with a, b co-prime. What do we get after squaring and rearranging?
quiz.explain: Squaring gives 3 = a²/b², so a² = 3b².
quiz.mistake: Squares only one side, or swaps a and b

quiz.q: In the proof that √2 is irrational, why do we start by taking a and b co-prime?
options: Because a and b must both be prime
So that a must be even
So that a and b are both odd
So that finding a common factor 2 gives a contradiction
quiz.explain: Any fraction can be reduced to lowest terms. If we then show 2 divides both a and b, that clashes with 'no common factor'.
quiz.mistake: Confuses 'co-prime' with 'both numbers are prime'

quiz.q: Which of these is rational?
quiz.explain: (3 + √5) − √5 = 3, which is rational. The others stay irrational.
quiz.mistake: Thinks any expression containing a square root must be irrational

quiz.q: Why is 6 + √2 irrational?
options: Because a rational number plus an irrational number is always irrational
Because every sum of numbers is irrational
quiz.explain: If 6 + √2 were rational, then √2 = (6 + √2) − 6 would be rational too — impossible.
quiz.mistake: Gives a reason that has nothing to do with rational/irrational

quiz.q: What is √3 × √12?
quiz.explain: √3 × √12 = √36 = 6. Two irrational numbers can multiply to give a rational number.
quiz.mistake: Adds the numbers under the root, or forgets to take the square root of 36

quiz.q: Kabir says, 'Both factors are irrational, so √5 × √5 must be irrational.' Is he right?
options: Yes, irrational × irrational is always irrational
quiz.explain: √5 × √5 = 5. The product of two irrationals can be rational.
quiz.mistake: Overgeneralises: thinks irrationals always multiply to irrationals

quiz.q: Which statement is ALWAYS true?
options: The sum of two irrational numbers is irrational
The product of two irrational numbers is irrational
A non-zero rational number times an irrational number is irrational
The square root of every whole number is irrational
quiz.explain: If q × x = r with q, r rational and q ≠ 0, then x = r/q is rational, a contradiction. The others fail: √2 + (−√2) = 0, √2 × √2 = 2, √9 = 3.
quiz.mistake: Treats a rule that works sometimes as one that always works

teach.ask: Gappu tilts his head: 'How can you be SURE √2 is not a fraction? Prove it to me!'
teach.praise: Wow, a proof by contradiction! √2 can't hide behind a fraction any more. Tweet!
teach.nudge: What do we pretend first, and what impossible thing do we reach at the end?

learn.hook: A zero of a polynomial is a secret number that makes the whole expression vanish — poof, it becomes 0!
points: The degree of a polynomial in x is the highest power of x in it: degree 1 is linear, 2 is quadratic, 3 is cubic.
A real number k is a zero of p(x) if p(k) = 0.
The zero of the linear polynomial ax + b (a ≠ 0) is −b/a.
A polynomial of degree n has at most n zeros.
Powers of x in a polynomial must be whole numbers, so 1/x or √x terms are not allowed. Coefficients like √3 are fine.

example.q: Find the zeros of p(x) = x² − 5x + 6.
steps: Find two numbers with product 6 and sum −5: they are −2 and −3

learn.reallife: Engineers find the zeros of polynomials to know exactly when a cricket ball's height becomes 0 — the moment it lands!

games.title: Linear, quadratic or cubic?
items: x² − 4
2x³ + x
x³
y² + 2y
t³ − t² + 1

games.title: Match the polynomial to its zero(s)

quiz.q: What is the degree of 4x³ − 7x⁵ + 2?
quiz.explain: The degree is the highest power of x. The term −7x⁵ has power 5.
quiz.mistake: Takes the power of the first term instead of the highest power

quiz.q: What is the zero of the polynomial 2x − 8?
quiz.explain: Set 2x − 8 = 0, so 2x = 8 and x = 4.
quiz.mistake: Takes the constant term as the zero, or gets the sign wrong

quiz.q: If p(x) = x² − 3x + 2, what is p(−1)?
quiz.mistake: Treats (−1)² as −1 or −3 × (−1) as −3

quiz.q: Which number is a zero of x² + x − 12?
quiz.explain: x² + x − 12 = (x + 4)(x − 3), so the zeros are −4 and 3. Check: 9 + 3 − 12 = 0.
steps: Two numbers with product −12 and sum 1: 4 and −3
quiz.mistake: Gets the signs of the zeros the wrong way round

quiz.q: At most how many zeros can a cubic polynomial have?
quiz.explain: A polynomial of degree n has at most n zeros. A cubic has degree 3.
quiz.mistake: Thinks every polynomial has 2 zeros like a quadratic

quiz.q: If x = 2 is a zero of x² + kx − 10, what is k?
quiz.explain: p(2) = 0 gives 4 + 2k − 10 = 0, so 2k = 6 and k = 3.
quiz.mistake: Makes a sign error while moving terms across

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT a polynomial?
quiz.explain: 1/x means x to the power −1, and powers in a polynomial must be whole numbers. A coefficient like √3 is allowed, and 7 is a constant polynomial.
quiz.mistake: Thinks a coefficient like √3 stops it being a polynomial

quiz.q: What is the zero of the linear polynomial ax + b, where a ≠ 0?
quiz.explain: ax + b = 0 gives ax = −b, so x = −b/a.
quiz.mistake: Forgets the minus sign when moving b across

teach.ask: Gappu scratches his head: 'What does it mean when someone says 3 is a zero of a polynomial?'
teach.praise: Tweet! Put the number in, and if the answer is 0, it's a zero. So simple!
teach.nudge: What do I do with the number, and what answer should I get?

learn.hook: Draw a polynomial and its zeros jump out — they are exactly where the graph meets the x-axis!
points: The zeros of p(x) are the x-coordinates of the points where the graph of y = p(x) meets the x-axis.
A linear polynomial ax + b (a ≠ 0) gives a straight line that cuts the x-axis exactly once.
A quadratic gives a U-shaped curve called a parabola. It may cut the x-axis twice, touch it once, or miss it completely — so it has 2, 1 or 0 zeros.
For y = ax² + bx + c, the parabola opens upwards if a > 0 and downwards if a < 0.
A cubic polynomial's graph meets the x-axis at least once and at most three times.

example.q: Where does the graph of y = x² − 4 meet the x-axis?
example.answer: At (−2, 0) and (2, 0); the zeros are −2 and 2

learn.reallife: The path of a water jet from a garden pipe is a parabola; its zeros tell where the water starts and where it lands.

games.title: Graph detective
items: Every quadratic polynomial has exactly two zeros.
Some parabolas never meet the x-axis, like y = x² + 1, so they have no zeros.
The graph of a linear polynomial ax + b (a ≠ 0) cuts the x-axis exactly once.
It is a slanted straight line, so it crosses the x-axis at one point, x = −b/a.
If a > 0, the parabola y = ax² + bx + c opens upwards.
A positive x² coefficient makes the U open upwards.
The point where a graph cuts the y-axis gives a zero of the polynomial.
Zeros are where the graph meets the x-axis, not the y-axis.
A cubic polynomial can have a graph that crosses the x-axis only once.
For example, y = x³ crosses the x-axis only at x = 0.
A parabola can cut the x-axis at three points.
A quadratic has at most 2 zeros, so its parabola meets the x-axis at most twice.

games.title: Match the graph to the number of zeros
pairs: Cubic curve crossing the x-axis three times

quiz.q: The graph of y = p(x) cuts the x-axis at (−3, 0), (1, 0) and (4, 0). How many zeros does p(x) have?
quiz.explain: Each point where the graph meets the x-axis gives one zero: −3, 1 and 4.
quiz.mistake: Counts the coordinates instead of the crossing points

quiz.q: The graph of a quadratic polynomial just touches the x-axis at one point. How many zeros does it have?
quiz.explain: The graph meets the x-axis at only one point, so there is exactly one zero (it is repeated).
quiz.mistake: Thinks every quadratic must show two zeros

quiz.q: Which way does the parabola y = −x² + 4 open?
quiz.explain: The coefficient of x² is −1, which is negative, so the parabola opens downwards.
quiz.mistake: Looks at the constant 4 instead of the sign of the x² term

quiz.q: At how many points does the graph of y = x² + 1 meet the x-axis?
quiz.explain: x² is never negative, so x² + 1 is always at least 1. The parabola stays above the x-axis and never meets it.
quiz.mistake: Assumes every parabola must cross the x-axis

quiz.q: A parabola meets the x-axis at (2, 0) and (5, 0). Which polynomial could it be?
quiz.explain: Zeros 2 and 5 give (x − 2)(x − 5) = x² − 7x + 10.
quiz.mistake: Uses (x + 2)(x + 5) and gets the middle sign wrong

quiz.q: Where does the line y = 2x − 6 cut the x-axis?
quiz.explain: On the x-axis y = 0, so 2x − 6 = 0 and x = 3. The point is (3, 0).
quiz.mistake: Writes the point as (0, 3) or uses the y-intercept −6

quiz.q: The graph of a polynomial cuts the x-axis at 4 different points. What is the smallest possible degree of the polynomial?
quiz.explain: A polynomial of degree n has at most n zeros. To have 4 zeros, the degree must be at least 4.
quiz.mistake: Forgets that the number of zeros cannot be more than the degree

quiz.q: At which point does the graph of y = x² − 6x + 9 touch the x-axis?
quiz.explain: x² − 6x + 9 = (x − 3)², which is 0 only at x = 3. So the parabola touches the x-axis at (3, 0).
quiz.mistake: Picks (0, 9), which is where the graph meets the y-axis

teach.ask: Gappu is holding a graph upside down: 'How can I find the zeros just by looking at this picture?'
teach.praise: Chirp! Look where the curve meets the x-axis and read the x values. Graphs are fun!
teach.nudge: Which axis should I look at, and which number of the point do I read?

learn.hook: You can find the sum and product of the zeros without ever finding the zeros — just peek at the coefficients!
points: If α and β are the zeros of ax² + bx + c (a ≠ 0), then α + β = −b/a.
And the product αβ = c/a.
A quadratic with zeros whose sum is S and product is P is k(x² − Sx + P), for any non-zero number k.
For a cubic ax³ + bx² + cx + d with zeros α, β, γ: α + β + γ = −b/a, αβ + βγ + γα = c/a and αβγ = −d/a.
Useful trick: α² + β² = (α + β)² − 2αβ.

example.q: Find the zeros of x² − 2x − 8 and check the relations with the coefficients.
steps: x² − 2x − 8 = (x − 4)(x + 2), so the zeros are 4 and −2
example.answer: Zeros 4 and −2; sum 2 = −b/a and product −8 = c/a

learn.reallife: Puzzle makers use these relations to build quadratics with nice whole-number answers for quiz contests.

quiz.q: What is the sum of the zeros of 3x² − 6x + 2?
quiz.mistake: Forgets the minus sign in −b/a

quiz.q: What is the product of the zeros of 4x² + 5x − 8?
quiz.explain: Product = c/a = −8/4 = −2.
quiz.mistake: Uses c alone without dividing by a

quiz.q: Which quadratic has zeros whose sum is −3 and product is 2?
quiz.explain: Use x² − (sum)x + product = x² − (−3)x + 2 = x² + 3x + 2. Its zeros are −1 and −2.
quiz.mistake: Writes the sum with the wrong sign

quiz.q: If α and β are the zeros of x² − 7x + 10, what is α² + β²?
quiz.explain: α + β = 7 and αβ = 10. So α² + β² = (α + β)² − 2αβ = 49 − 20 = 29. (The zeros are 2 and 5: 4 + 25 = 29.)
quiz.mistake: Thinks α² + β² = (α + β)², or adds 2αβ instead of subtracting

quiz.q: One zero of x² − 5x + k is 2. What is k?
quiz.explain: The sum of the zeros is 5, so the other zero is 3. Then k = product = 2 × 3 = 6.
quiz.mistake: Gives the other zero (3) instead of k

quiz.q: The zeros of 2x² + kx − 6 add up to 3. What is k?
quiz.mistake: Forgets the minus sign in −b/a and gets k = 6

quiz.q: If α and β are the zeros of x² − 6x + 4, what is 1/α + 1/β?
quiz.mistake: Turns the fraction upside down (αβ divided by α + β)

quiz.q: What is the product of the zeros of the cubic x³ − 4x² + x + 6?
quiz.explain: For a cubic, αβγ = −d/a = −6/1 = −6. (The zeros are −1, 2 and 3, and −1 × 2 × 3 = −6.)
quiz.mistake: Uses the quadratic rule c/a, or forgets the minus sign in −d/a

teach.ask: Gappu peeks at x² − 5x + 6: 'Can you tell me the sum and product of its zeros without solving it?'
teach.praise: Wow! Sum is −b/a and product is c/a. Magic without solving. Tweet tweet!
teach.nudge: Which coefficients do I divide to get the sum, and which for the product?

chapters.title: Pair of Linear Equations in Two Variables

learn.hook: Two straight lines on a graph can meet once, never meet, or sit right on top of each other — and each story tells you about the answer!
points: A pair of linear equations is a₁x + b₁y + c₁ = 0 and a₂x + b₂y + c₂ = 0. Each one is a straight line on a graph.
If the lines intersect at one point, that point is the unique solution. The pair is consistent.
If the lines are parallel, there is no solution. The pair is inconsistent.
If the lines coincide (are the same line), there are infinitely many solutions. The pair is dependent and consistent.
Shortcut without drawing: a₁/a₂ ≠ b₁/b₂ means one solution; a₁/a₂ = b₁/b₂ ≠ c₁/c₂ means parallel lines; a₁/a₂ = b₁/b₂ = c₁/c₂ means the lines coincide.

example.q: Solve x + y = 5 and x − y = 1 graphically.
steps: For x + y = 5, plot (0, 5) and (5, 0) and join them
For x − y = 1, plot (1, 0) and (0, −1) and join them

learn.reallife: If two auto-rickshaw fare plans are drawn as lines, the crossing point shows the distance at which both plans cost the same.

games.title: Lines on a graph
items: A pair of parallel lines has no common solution.
Parallel lines never meet, so no point lies on both.
If a₁/a₂ = b₁/b₂ = c₁/c₂, the two lines coincide.
One equation is just a multiple of the other, so they are the same line.
An inconsistent pair has exactly one solution.
Inconsistent means there is no solution at all.
x + y = 3 and 2x + 2y = 6 have infinitely many solutions.
The second equation is 2 times the first, so the lines coincide.
Two different straight lines can meet at exactly two points.
Two different straight lines meet at most once.
The pair x = 3 and y = 2 has the unique solution (3, 2).
x = 3 is a vertical line and y = 2 is a horizontal line; they cross only at (3, 2).

quiz.q: The lines 2x + 3y = 9 and 4x + 6y = 18 are…
quiz.explain: 2/4 = 3/6 = 9/18 = 1/2. All three ratios are equal, so the lines coincide.
quiz.mistake: Sees equal a and b ratios and says parallel without checking c

quiz.q: For which values of k do kx + 2y = 5 and 3x + y = 1 have a unique solution?
quiz.explain: A unique solution needs a₁/a₂ ≠ b₁/b₂, so k/3 ≠ 2/1, which means k ≠ 6.
quiz.mistake: Uses '=' instead of '≠' for the unique-solution condition

quiz.q: For what value of k are the lines x + 2y = 3 and 3x + ky = 7 parallel?
quiz.explain: Parallel lines need 1/3 = 2/k, so k = 6. Also 3/7 ≠ 1/3, so the lines do not coincide.
quiz.mistake: Cross-multiplies wrongly and gets 2/3

quiz.q: The lines x + y = 6 and x − y = 2 are drawn on a graph. Where do they meet?
quiz.explain: Adding the equations gives 2x = 8, so x = 4 and y = 2. Check: 4 + 2 = 6 and 4 − 2 = 2.
quiz.mistake: Swaps the x- and y-coordinates

quiz.q: Riya draws two lines that never meet, however far she extends them. The pair of equations is…
quiz.explain: Lines that never meet are parallel, so there is no solution. Such a pair is called inconsistent.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the words consistent and inconsistent

quiz.q: Where does the line 2x + y = 6 meet the y-axis?
quiz.explain: On the y-axis x = 0, so y = 6. The point is (0, 6).
quiz.mistake: Finds where the line meets the x-axis instead, (3, 0)

quiz.q: How many solutions do 3x − 5y = 2 and 6x − 10y = 4 have?
quiz.explain: 3/6 = −5/−10 = 2/4 = 1/2, so the lines coincide and every point on the line is a solution.
quiz.mistake: Thinks a pair of linear equations always has exactly one solution

quiz.q: Which pair has exactly one solution?
quiz.explain: For x + y = 5 and 2x − y = 1, a₁/a₂ = 1/2 and b₁/b₂ = 1/(−1) = −1 are different, so the lines intersect once (at (2, 3)).
quiz.mistake: Does not compare the ratios a₁/a₂ and b₁/b₂

teach.ask: Gappu draws two lines with a crayon: 'How do these lines tell me how many answers the equations have?'
teach.praise: Cheep! Meeting once, never meeting, or being the same line — I get it now!
teach.nudge: What happens to the answer if the lines are parallel, or the same line?

learn.hook: Make one variable 'wear the costume' of the other, swap it in, and the puzzle shrinks to one variable!
points: Step 1: from one equation, write one variable in terms of the other (for example y = 2x − 4).
Step 2: substitute this into the other equation, so it has only one variable.
Step 3: solve that equation, then put the value back to find the other variable.
Always check your answer in both original equations.
If you end with a true statement like 6 = 6, there are infinitely many solutions. If you get a false one like 0 = 4, there is no solution.

example.q: Kabir buys 2 pens and 3 notebooks for ₹80. A notebook costs ₹10 more than a pen. Find each price.
steps: Let a pen cost ₹p and a notebook ₹n. Then n = p + 10 and 2p + 3n = 80

learn.reallife: Shopkeepers in a market use this kind of reasoning when one price is 'so much more' than another.

games.title: Put the substitution steps in order
items: From 2x − y = 4, write y = 2x − 4
Substitute: x + 2(2x − 4) = 7

items.q: y = 2x and x + y = 9. Find x
y = x + 1 and x + y = 7. Find y
x = 2y and x + y = 15. Find x
y = 3x and x + y = 8. Find y
x = y + 2 and x + y = 10. Find x
y = 5 − x and 2x + y = 8. Find x

quiz.q: Solve x + y = 10 and x − y = 2. What is x?
quiz.explain: From x − y = 2, x = y + 2. Then (y + 2) + y = 10, so y = 4 and x = 6.
quiz.mistake: Gives the value of y instead of x

quiz.q: If y = 2x − 3 and 3x + y = 12, what is x?
quiz.explain: 3x + (2x − 3) = 12 gives 5x = 15, so x = 3 (and y = 3).
quiz.mistake: Moves −3 across without changing its sign, getting 5x = 9

quiz.q: Substituting y = 4 − x into 2x + 3y = 10 gives which equation?
quiz.explain: 3y = 3(4 − x) = 12 − 3x, so the equation becomes 2x + 12 − 3x = 10.
quiz.mistake: Multiplies only the first term inside the bracket by 3

quiz.q: Meena is 3 times as old as her brother. The sum of their ages is 24 years. How old is Meena?
quiz.explain: Let the brother be b years. Meena = 3b, so 3b + b = 24, b = 6 and Meena is 18.
quiz.mistake: Gives the brother's age instead of Meena's

quiz.q: 2 samosas and 1 cup of tea cost ₹40. 1 samosa and 1 cup of tea cost ₹25. What does one samosa cost?
quiz.explain: From the second equation t = 25 − s. Then 2s + 25 − s = 40, so s = 15 (and tea costs ₹10).
quiz.mistake: Gives the price of the tea

quiz.q: While solving a pair by substitution, Aisha ends up with 6 = 6. What does this mean?
options: The pair has infinitely many solutions
quiz.explain: A statement that is always true means both equations describe the same line, so every point on it is a solution.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the number 6 is the value of a variable

quiz.q: While solving a pair, Arjun's working ends with 0 = 4. What does this tell him?
options: The pair has infinitely many solutions
quiz.explain: 0 = 4 is false, so no values of x and y satisfy both equations. The lines are parallel.
quiz.mistake: Reads the numbers in a false statement as the solution

quiz.q: Two numbers add up to 35 and one is 7 more than the other. What is the larger number?
quiz.explain: Let the smaller be x. Then x + (x + 7) = 35, so x = 14 and the larger is 21.
quiz.mistake: Gives the smaller number, or just halves 35

teach.ask: Gappu has two equations and is stuck: 'How does the substitution trick work?'
teach.praise: Tweet! Write one in terms of the other, put it in, and solve. Easy-peasy!
teach.nudge: After I write y in terms of x, where do I put it?

learn.hook: Line up two equations, add or subtract, and watch one variable vanish like a magic trick!
points: Multiply one or both equations so that one variable has the same (or opposite) coefficient in both.
Subtract the equations if the coefficients are the same, or add them if they are opposite, to eliminate that variable.
Solve for the remaining variable, then substitute back to find the other one.
For word problems: name the two unknowns, write two equations from the two facts given, then solve.
Check that your answer makes sense in the story — a negative number of notes is a sign of an error!

example.q: Solve 3x + 2y = 11 and 2x − 2y = 4.
steps: The y terms are +2y and −2y, so add the equations

learn.reallife: Cricket kit shops, fruit sellers and ticket counters all face 'two unknown prices, two bills' puzzles like these.

items.text: To eliminate y from 2x + 3y = 8 and x − y = 1, multiply the second equation by ___
Adding x + y = 7 and x − y = 3 gives 2x = ___
Subtracting x + y = 5 from x + 2y = 9 gives y = ___
From 3x + y = 10 and 3x − y = 8, x = ___

games.title: Match the story to its equations
pairs: Two numbers add to 50 and differ by 10
A fraction's numerator and denominator add to 12; the denominator is twice the numerator
A bat costs ₹300 more than a ball; together they cost ₹500

quiz.q: Solve 2x + y = 7 and x − y = 2. What is y?
quiz.explain: Adding the equations gives 3x = 9, so x = 3. Then y = 7 − 2 × 3 = 1.
quiz.mistake: Stops after finding x and gives it as y

quiz.q: Solve 3x + 4y = 10 and 3x − 2y = 4. What is x?
quiz.explain: Subtract: (3x + 4y) − (3x − 2y) = 6y = 6, so y = 1. Then 3x = 10 − 4 = 6, so x = 2.
quiz.mistake: Treats 4y − (−2y) as 2y instead of 6y

quiz.q: Which step eliminates x from x + 3y = 9 and 2x + y = 8?
options: Multiply the second equation by 3 and add
Multiply the first equation by 2 and subtract
Subtract the equations as they are
quiz.explain: Multiplying the first by 2 gives 2x + 6y = 18. Subtracting 2x + y = 8 removes x: 5y = 10.
quiz.mistake: Adds or subtracts before making the x coefficients equal

quiz.q: Harpreet has 25 notes of ₹10 and ₹20 worth ₹350 in all. How many ₹20 notes does she have?
quiz.explain: x + y = 25 and 10x + 20y = 350, so x + 2y = 35. Subtracting gives y = 10 ₹20 notes (and 15 ₹10 notes).
quiz.mistake: Gives the number of ₹10 notes instead

quiz.q: 2 cricket bats and 3 balls cost ₹1300. 1 bat and 2 balls cost ₹700. What does one bat cost?
quiz.explain: Double the second bill: 2b + 4c = 1400. Subtract the first: c = 100. Then b = 700 − 200 = 500.
quiz.mistake: Gives the price of a ball

quiz.q: The numerator and denominator of a fraction add up to 13, and the denominator is 3 more than the numerator. What is the fraction?
quiz.explain: x + y = 13 and y − x = 3. Adding gives 2y = 16, so y = 8 and x = 5. The fraction is 5/8.
quiz.mistake: Writes the fraction upside down

quiz.q: The digits of a two-digit number add up to 9. Reversing the digits increases the number by 27. What is the number?
quiz.explain: Let the number be 10a + b. Then a + b = 9 and (10b + a) − (10a + b) = 27, so b − a = 3. Solving: b = 6, a = 3, giving 36. Check: 63 − 36 = 27 ✓
quiz.mistake: Gives the reversed number 63

quiz.q: Solve 4x + 3y = 26 and 2x − 3y = 4. What is x + y?
quiz.explain: Adding gives 6x = 30, so x = 5. Then 3y = 26 − 20 = 6, so y = 2. x + y = 7.
quiz.mistake: Gives only x (5) instead of x + y

teach.ask: Gappu stares at 3x + 2y = 11 and 2x − 2y = 4: 'How can I make one letter disappear?'
teach.praise: Chirp chirp! Make the numbers match, add or subtract, and one letter vanishes. Magic!
teach.nudge: What must be the same in both equations before I add or subtract them?

learn.hook: Split the middle term, pull out common factors, and a quadratic breaks neatly into two easy pieces!
points: A quadratic equation has the standard form ax² + bx + c = 0 with a ≠ 0.
A root is a value of x that makes the equation true. A quadratic equation has at most two roots.
To factorise ax² + bx + c, find two numbers whose product is ac and whose sum is b, and use them to split the middle term.
If (x − p)(x − q) = 0, then x = p or x = q, because a product is zero only when one factor is zero.
Never divide both sides by x — you may lose the root x = 0. Bring all terms to one side instead.

example.q: Solve 2x² − 5x + 3 = 0 by factorisation.
steps: ac = 2 × 3 = 6; two numbers with product 6 and sum −5 are −2 and −3

learn.reallife: Designers of a rectangular rangoli or garden with a fixed area often end up with a quadratic equation to find its sides.

games.title: Match the equation to its roots
Quadratic or not?
items: x(x + 1) = x² + 5 is a quadratic equation.
The x² terms cancel, leaving x = 5, which is linear.
x² = 0 has the root 0.
0² = 0, so x = 0 is a root (repeated).
In 3x² − 7 = 0, the value of b is 0.
There is no x term, so b = 0.
To factorise x² + 7x + 12, we need two numbers with product 12 and sum 7.
3 and 4 work: (x + 3)(x + 4).
If (x − 4)(x + 1) = 0, then x = −4 or x = 1.
Each factor is zero when x = 4 or x = −1.
A quadratic equation can have three different roots.
A quadratic equation has at most two roots.

quiz.q: Which of these is a quadratic equation?
quiz.explain: (x + 1)² = 2x + 5 becomes x² + 2x + 1 = 2x + 5, that is x² − 4 = 0, which has degree 2. In x² + 3x = x² − 1 the x² terms cancel, leaving a linear equation.
quiz.mistake: Judges by the look of the equation without simplifying it

quiz.q: What are the roots of x² − 7x + 12 = 0?
quiz.explain: −3 and −4 have product 12 and sum −7, so x² − 7x + 12 = (x − 3)(x − 4). The roots are 3 and 4.
quiz.mistake: Picks a pair with product 12 but the wrong sum, or flips the signs

quiz.q: What are the roots of 6x² − x − 2 = 0?
quiz.explain: ac = −12; the numbers −4 and 3 have product −12 and sum −1. So 6x² − 4x + 3x − 2 = 2x(3x − 2) + 1(3x − 2) = (2x + 1)(3x − 2).
quiz.mistake: Gets the signs of the roots the wrong way round

quiz.q: The product of two consecutive positive integers is 132. What is the smaller integer?
quiz.explain: x(x + 1) = 132 gives x² + x − 132 = 0 = (x + 12)(x − 11). Since x is positive, x = 11 (and 11 × 12 = 132).
quiz.mistake: Gives the larger integer, or keeps the negative root

quiz.q: A rectangular mat is 4 m longer than it is wide, and its area is 60 m². What is its width?
quiz.explain: b(b + 4) = 60 gives b² + 4b − 60 = 0 = (b + 10)(b − 6). Width cannot be negative, so b = 6 m (length 10 m).
quiz.mistake: Gives the length (10 m) instead of the width

quiz.q: If x = 2 is a root of x² + kx + 6 = 0, what is k?
quiz.mistake: Loses the minus sign when moving 10 across

quiz.q: Kabir solves x² = 5x by dividing both sides by x and gets x = 5. Which root did he lose?
quiz.explain: x² − 5x = 0 gives x(x − 5) = 0, so x = 0 or x = 5. Dividing by x threw away x = 0.
quiz.mistake: Divides by a variable that could be zero

quiz.q: What are the roots of 4x² − 4x + 1 = 0?
quiz.explain: 4x² − 4x + 1 = (2x − 1)², so 2x − 1 = 0 twice. Both roots are 1/2.
quiz.mistake: Gets the sign of the root wrong

teach.ask: Gappu waves a quadratic equation: 'How do I break x² − 5x + 6 = 0 into pieces and find x?'
teach.praise: Tweet! Split the middle term using product and sum, then set each bracket to zero. Brilliant!
teach.nudge: Which two numbers do I look for, and what do I do with each bracket?

learn.hook: Can't factorise? No problem! One formula cracks every quadratic equation that has real roots.
points: For ax² + bx + c = 0 (a ≠ 0), the roots are x = [−b ± √(b² − 4ac)] / 2a.
The quantity D = b² − 4ac is called the discriminant.
The formula gives real roots only when D ≥ 0.
First write the equation in standard form, then read a, b and c with their signs.
In word problems, reject roots that make no sense, like a negative speed or length.

example.q: Solve 2x² + x − 6 = 0 using the quadratic formula.

learn.reallife: Rocket scientists and bridge engineers use the quadratic formula to find times and lengths that don't factorise nicely.

items.text: For x² + 4x − 5 = 0, D = b² − 4ac = ___
In the quadratic formula, the denominator is ___
The roots of x² − 2x − 1 = 0 are 1 ± ___

quiz.q: Use the quadratic formula to solve x² − 2x − 15 = 0.
quiz.mistake: Uses +b instead of −b in the formula

quiz.q: What is the discriminant of 3x² − 4x − 4 = 0?
quiz.mistake: Treats −4ac as −48 instead of +48

quiz.q: What are the roots of x² + 4x + 1 = 0?
quiz.mistake: Forgets to divide every term by 2a, or drops the minus on b

quiz.q: What is the larger root of 2x² − 3x − 5 = 0?
quiz.explain: D = 9 + 40 = 49, so x = (3 ± 7)/4, giving 5/2 or −1. The larger is 5/2.
quiz.mistake: Divides by a instead of 2a

quiz.q: Before using the formula on x² = 3x + 10, what are a, b and c?
quiz.explain: Rewrite it as x² − 3x − 10 = 0. Then a = 1, b = −3 and c = −10.
quiz.mistake: Reads a, b, c before bringing everything to one side

quiz.q: A train covers 300 km at a steady speed. If it went 10 km/h faster, the trip would take 1 hour less. What is its speed in km/h?
quiz.mistake: Gives the faster speed 60 km/h instead of the actual speed

quiz.q: A number plus its reciprocal equals 10/3. What could the number be?
quiz.mistake: Makes a sign error with the reciprocal

quiz.q: What is the repeated root of 9x² − 6x + 1 = 0?
quiz.mistake: Forgets the minus in −b/2a, or divides by a only

teach.ask: Gappu can't factorise 2x² + x − 6 = 0: 'Is there a formula that always works?'
teach.praise: Chirp! −b plus or minus root of the discriminant, all over 2a. I'll never be stuck again!
teach.nudge: What goes under the square root, and what do I divide by?

learn.hook: Before solving, the discriminant whispers a secret: two roots, one root, or none at all!
points: D = b² − 4ac decides the nature of the roots of ax² + bx + c = 0.
D > 0: two distinct real roots.
D = 0: two equal real roots, each equal to −b/2a.
D < 0: no real roots.
On a graph, D > 0 means the parabola cuts the x-axis twice, D = 0 means it touches once, and D < 0 means it does not meet the x-axis.

example.q: Find k so that kx² − 6x + 1 = 0 has two equal roots.

learn.reallife: Before building, an architect can check with the discriminant whether a park with a given perimeter and area is even possible.

games.title: Discriminant true or false
items: If D < 0, the equation has no real roots.
The square root of a negative number is not real.
If D = 0, each root equals −b/2a.
With D = 0 the ± part disappears, leaving −b/2a.
x² + 4 = 0 has the real roots 2 and −2.
D = 0 − 16 < 0, so it has no real roots. 2² + 4 = 8, not 0.
Every quadratic equation has at least one real root.
x² + 1 = 0 has none, since D = −4.
If a and c have opposite signs, the equation has two distinct real roots.
Then −4ac is positive, so D = b² − 4ac > 0.
If D > 0, the parabola touches the x-axis at exactly one point.
D > 0 means it cuts the x-axis at two points.

quiz.q: What is the nature of the roots of 2x² − 4x + 3 = 0?
options: One positive and one negative root
quiz.explain: D = 16 − 24 = −8, which is negative, so there are no real roots.
quiz.mistake: Forgets to multiply by 4 in 4ac

quiz.q: For what positive value of k does x² + kx + 16 = 0 have equal roots?
quiz.explain: Equal roots need D = 0: k² − 64 = 0, so k = 8 (taking the positive value).
quiz.mistake: Forgets the 4 in 4ac and gets k = 4

quiz.q: What is the discriminant of 5x² − 3x + 1 = 0?
quiz.mistake: Adds 4ac instead of subtracting it

quiz.q: For which values of k does 2x² + 3x + k = 0 have no real roots?
quiz.explain: No real roots need D < 0: 9 − 8k < 0, so k > 9/8.
quiz.mistake: Flips the inequality sign

quiz.q: kx² + 4x + 1 = 0 has equal roots. What is the repeated root?
quiz.explain: D = 16 − 4k = 0 gives k = 4. The root is −b/2a = −4/8 = −1/2.
quiz.mistake: Drops the minus sign in −b/2a

quiz.q: Can a rectangular park have perimeter 40 m and area 120 m²?
options: No, because the discriminant is negative
No, because the area is too small
quiz.explain: l + b = 20 and lb = 120 give l² − 20l + 120 = 0. D = 400 − 480 = −80 < 0, so no such park exists. (12 × 10 has perimeter 44, and 15 × 8 has perimeter 46.)
quiz.mistake: Checks only the area and forgets the perimeter

quiz.q: Which equation has two distinct real roots?
quiz.explain: For 2x² + 5x − 3 = 0, D = 25 + 24 = 49 > 0. x² + x + 1 has D = −3, x² − 4x + 4 has D = 0 and x² + 3 has D = −12.
quiz.mistake: Thinks a perfect square like x² − 4x + 4 gives two different roots

quiz.q: A quadratic equation has two equal real roots. What does the graph of y = ax² + bx + c do?
options: Cuts the x-axis at two points
Touches the x-axis at exactly one point
quiz.explain: Equal roots mean D = 0, so the parabola just touches the x-axis at x = −b/2a.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up equal roots with two distinct roots

teach.ask: Gappu wonders: 'How can I tell how many roots a quadratic has without solving it?'
teach.praise: Tweet tweet! Positive D gives two roots, zero gives equal roots, negative gives none. Super!
teach.nudge: What happens when the discriminant is zero, or negative?

learn.hook: Climbing stairs, saving pocket money every week, or a taxi meter ticking up — all follow the same steady pattern!
points: An arithmetic progression (AP) is a list of numbers where each term is got by adding a fixed number to the previous term.
This fixed number is the common difference d = a₂ − a₁ = a₃ − a₂ = … It can be positive, negative, zero or a fraction.
An AP with first term a looks like a, a + d, a + 2d, a + 3d, …
To test for an AP, check that the difference between every pair of consecutive terms is the same.
An AP can be finite (it stops) or infinite (it goes on forever).

example.q: Is 3, 7, 11, 15, … an AP? If yes, find the next term.
steps: The difference is always 4, so it is an AP with d = 4
example.answer: Yes, d = 4; the next term is 19

learn.reallife: If Joseph puts ₹20 more in his piggy bank each week than the week before, his weekly savings form an AP.

games.title: Build the AP
games.prompt: Terms of the AP with a = 4 and d = −3, first to fifth

quiz.q: What is the common difference of 15, 11, 7, 3, …?
quiz.explain: d = 11 − 15 = −4. The terms go down by 4 each time.
quiz.mistake: Subtracts the wrong way round (15 − 11 = 4)

quiz.q: What is the next term of 2.5, 4, 5.5, …?
quiz.explain: d = 4 − 2.5 = 1.5, so the next term is 5.5 + 1.5 = 7.
quiz.mistake: Adds 1 instead of the common difference 1.5

quiz.q: Which of these lists is an AP?
quiz.explain: 5, 5, 5, 5 has common difference 0, which is allowed. The others have changing differences.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the common difference cannot be zero

quiz.q: If 2k + 1, 13 and 5k − 3 are three consecutive terms of an AP, what is k?
quiz.explain: In an AP, the middle term is the average of its neighbours: 2 × 13 = (2k + 1) + (5k − 3). So 26 = 7k − 2 and k = 4. The terms are 9, 13, 17.
quiz.mistake: Forgets the −2 and writes 7k = 26

quiz.q: Riya saves ₹50 in week 1, ₹75 in week 2 and ₹100 in week 3, continuing the pattern. Which describes her savings?
quiz.explain: The first term is 50 and each week she saves ₹25 more: 75 − 50 = 100 − 75 = 25.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the first term and the common difference

quiz.q: What is the fourth term of the AP with a = −3 and d = 1/2?
quiz.explain: The fourth term is a + 3d = −3 + 3/2 = −3/2.
quiz.mistake: Adds 4d instead of 3d

quiz.q: A taxi charges ₹30 for the first km and ₹12 for each extra km. What is the fare for 3 km?
quiz.explain: The fares 30, 42, 54, … form an AP with d = 12. For 3 km: 30 + 2 × 12 = ₹54.
quiz.mistake: Charges ₹12 for all 3 km on top of ₹30

items: 1 km
2 km
3 km

quiz.q: Which statement about every AP is TRUE?
options: The common difference must be positive
The difference between consecutive terms is constant
The ratio of consecutive terms is constant
An AP must have infinitely many terms
quiz.explain: That is the definition of an AP. The difference can be negative or zero, and an AP can be finite.
quiz.mistake: Confuses a constant difference with a constant ratio

teach.ask: Gappu sees 3, 7, 11, 15: 'Is this an AP? How do I check?'
teach.praise: Chirp chirp! Subtract each term from the next, and if the gap is always the same, it's an AP!
teach.nudge: What do I subtract, and what must stay the same?

topics.title: The nth term of an AP

learn.hook: Want the 100th term without writing 99 terms first? One short formula jumps straight there!
points: The nth term of an AP is aₙ = a + (n − 1)d.
You add d only (n − 1) times, because the first term already has no d.
Number of terms in a finite AP: n = (l − a)/d + 1, where l is the last term.
The nth term from the end is l − (n − 1)d.
A number is a term of the AP only if the n you get is a positive whole number.

example.q: Find the 40th term of 5, 9, 13, …

learn.reallife: Seats in a stadium often increase by the same number in every row — the nth-term formula tells how many seats are in row 30.

items.text: In aₙ = a + (n − 1)d, d stands for the ___
The 3rd term of an AP is a + ___
If a = 7 and d = 3, then a₄ = ___
The number of two-digit numbers divisible by 7 is ___

quiz.q: What is the 25th term of 2, 7, 12, …?
quiz.mistake: Uses n instead of n − 1 and gets 127

quiz.q: Which term of the AP 3, 8, 13, … is 78?
quiz.mistake: Forgets to add 1 at the end

quiz.q: Is 301 a term of the AP 5, 11, 17, 23, …?
options: No, because (301 − 5)/6 is not a whole number
quiz.explain: For 301 to be a term, (301 − 5)/6 = 296/6 must be a whole number. It is 49.33…, so 301 is not a term.
quiz.mistake: Rounds n to a whole number instead of checking

quiz.q: The 4th term of an AP is 14 and the 9th term is 34. What is d?
quiz.explain: From the 4th to the 9th term we add d five times: 5d = 34 − 14 = 20, so d = 4.
quiz.mistake: Divides by 9 − 4 + 1 = 6 or forgets to divide at all

quiz.q: The 3rd term of an AP is 12 and the 7th term is 28. What is the first term?
quiz.mistake: Subtracts only one d from the 3rd term

quiz.q: How many three-digit numbers are divisible by 6?
quiz.mistake: Forgets the +1 in the counting formula

quiz.q: What is the 10th term from the end of the AP 3, 8, 13, …, 253?
quiz.explain: From the end, the AP goes 253, 248, … with d = −5. 10th term = 253 − 9 × 5 = 208.
quiz.mistake: Finds the 10th term from the start (48) instead

quiz.q: Kabir's salary starts at ₹20,000 a month and rises by ₹1,500 every year. In which year will it first be ₹35,000 a month?
quiz.mistake: Forgets that the first year has no raise and answers 10

teach.ask: Gappu wants the 50th term of 2, 5, 8, …: 'Do I really have to write all 50?'
teach.praise: Tweet! First term plus (n − 1) common differences. I can jump to any term now!
teach.nudge: Why do I multiply d by n − 1 and not by n?

topics.title: Sum of n terms of an AP

learn.hook: Young Gauss added 1 to 100 in seconds by pairing numbers — learn his trick and add any AP in a flash!
points: The sum of the first n terms is Sₙ = n/2 [2a + (n − 1)d].
If you know the last term l, use Sₙ = n/2 (a + l).
Sum of the first n natural numbers: 1 + 2 + … + n = n(n + 1)/2.
The nth term can be found from sums: aₙ = Sₙ − Sₙ₋₁.

a₂ = S₂ − S₁ = 4 − 1 = 3.

The sum of the first 10 terms of 1, 1, 1, … is 1.
Ten terms of 1 add up to 10.

learn.hook: A photo and its enlarged poster look exactly alike, only bigger — that is similarity!
points: Congruent figures have the same shape and the same size. Similar figures have the same shape but not necessarily the same size.
Two polygons with the same number of sides are similar if their corresponding angles are equal AND their corresponding sides are in the same ratio.
All circles are similar, all squares are similar and all equilateral triangles are similar.
Every pair of congruent figures is similar, but similar figures need not be congruent.
In ΔABC ~ ΔPQR the order matters: A ↔ P, B ↔ Q, C ↔ R, so AB/PQ = BC/QR = CA/RP.

example.q: ΔABC ~ ΔPQR with AB = 6 cm, BC = 8 cm and PQ = 9 cm. Find QR.
steps: Corresponding sides are in the same ratio: AB/PQ = BC/QR

learn.reallife: Maps, building models and the zoom on your phone camera all make figures similar to the real thing.

games.title: Same shape check
items: All circles are similar.
Any circle is just a scaled copy of another.
All rectangles are similar.
A 1 × 2 rectangle and a 1 × 5 rectangle have different shapes.
Two congruent figures are always similar.
They have the same shape (scale factor 1).
Two similar figures are always congruent.
Similar figures can be of different sizes.
All rhombuses are similar.
Their angles can be different, for example a square and a thin diamond.
For two polygons to be similar, equal angles alone are always enough.
A square and a long rectangle have equal angles but are not similar. Sides must be proportional too (triangles are a special case).

quiz.q: ΔABC ~ ΔDEF with AB = 4 cm, DE = 6 cm and BC = 5 cm. What is EF?
quiz.explain: AB/DE = BC/EF, so 4/6 = 5/EF and EF = 5 × 6 ÷ 4 = 7.5 cm.
quiz.mistake: Adds the difference 2 cm instead of using the ratio

quiz.q: Which pair of figures is ALWAYS similar?
quiz.explain: All squares have 90° angles and four equal sides, so one is always a scaled copy of the other.
quiz.mistake: Thinks equal angles alone make any polygons similar

quiz.q: A 10 cm × 15 cm photo is enlarged so that the 10 cm side becomes 25 cm. What does the 15 cm side become?
quiz.explain: The scale factor is 25/10 = 2.5, so the other side becomes 15 × 2.5 = 37.5 cm.
quiz.mistake: Adds 15 cm to the side instead of multiplying by the scale factor

quiz.q: ΔPQR ~ ΔXYZ, with ∠P = 50° and ∠Q = 70°. What is ∠Z?
quiz.explain: ∠Z corresponds to ∠R, and ∠R = 180° − 50° − 70° = 60°.
quiz.mistake: Matches the angles in the wrong order

quiz.q: Which conditions make two polygons with the same number of sides similar?
options: Corresponding angles equal and corresponding sides in the same ratio
quiz.explain: Both conditions are needed for polygons in general: equal corresponding angles and proportional corresponding sides.
quiz.mistake: Thinks one condition is always enough for any polygon

quiz.q: The scale factor from ΔABC to ΔPQR is 3. The perimeter of ΔABC is 12 cm. What is the perimeter of ΔPQR?
quiz.explain: Every side is multiplied by 3, so the perimeter is multiplied by 3: 12 × 3 = 36 cm.
quiz.mistake: Adds 3 to the perimeter or divides by 3

quiz.q: If ΔABC ~ ΔQRP, which angle is equal to ∠B?
quiz.explain: Read the letters in order: A ↔ Q, B ↔ R, C ↔ P. So ∠B = ∠R.
quiz.mistake: Matches letters by position in the alphabet instead of by order in the statement

quiz.q: On a map, 1 cm stands for 5 km. A road is 3.6 cm long on the map. How long is the real road?
quiz.explain: The map is similar to the real place with scale 1 : 5 km, so 3.6 × 5 = 18 km.
quiz.mistake: Adds 5 instead of multiplying by the scale

teach.ask: Gappu holds a small and a big photo of himself: 'Are these two pictures similar or congruent?'
teach.praise: Tweet! Same shape, maybe different size, with equal angles and sides in the same ratio. Similar!
teach.nudge: What must be the same, and what can be different, for two figures to be similar?

learn.hook: Draw a line parallel to one side of a triangle and it slices the other two sides in exactly the same ratio!
points: Basic Proportionality Theorem (Thales theorem): if a line parallel to one side of a triangle meets the other two sides at distinct points, it divides those sides in the same ratio.
In ΔABC with D on AB, E on AC and DE ∥ BC: AD/DB = AE/EC.
It also follows that AD/AB = AE/AC.
Converse: if a line divides two sides of a triangle in the same ratio, it is parallel to the third side.
Special case: the line through the midpoint of one side, parallel to another side, passes through the midpoint of the third side.

example.q: In ΔABC, DE ∥ BC with D on AB and E on AC. AD = 3 cm, DB = 4 cm and AE = 4.5 cm. Find EC.

learn.reallife: Carpenters making an A-frame stand fix crossbars parallel to the base; BPT tells them exactly where each bar must meet the two slanting legs.

quiz.q: In ΔABC, DE ∥ BC with AD = 6 cm, DB = 9 cm and AE = 8 cm. What is EC?
quiz.explain: AD/DB = AE/EC gives 6/9 = 8/EC, so EC = 8 × 9 ÷ 6 = 12 cm.
quiz.mistake: Flips the ratio and gets 8 × 6 ÷ 9 ≈ 5.33

quiz.q: In ΔABC, D is on AB and E is on AC with AD = 3, DB = 5, AE = 4.5 and EC = 7.5. Is DE ∥ BC?
options: No, because the sides are not equal
Yes, by the converse of BPT
quiz.explain: AD/DB = 3/5 = 0.6 and AE/EC = 4.5/7.5 = 0.6. The ratios are equal, so DE ∥ BC by the converse of BPT.
quiz.mistake: Expects the pieces to be equal rather than in the same ratio

quiz.q: In ΔABC, DE ∥ BC and AD/DB = 2/3. If AC = 20 cm, what is AE?
quiz.explain: AE/EC = 2/3, so AE is 2 parts out of 5 parts of AC: AE = 2/5 × 20 = 8 cm.
quiz.mistake: Uses 2/3 of AC instead of 2/5

quiz.q: In ΔABC, DE ∥ BC with AD = x, DB = x − 3, AE = x + 3 and EC = x − 2. Find x.
quiz.mistake: Makes a sign error when expanding (x + 3)(x − 3)

quiz.q: In ΔPQR, ST ∥ QR with S on PQ and T on PR. If PS/SQ = 3/4, what is PT/PR?
quiz.explain: PT/TR = 3/4, so PT is 3 parts of the 7 parts of PR: PT/PR = 3/7.
quiz.mistake: Confuses the part-to-part ratio with the part-to-whole ratio

quiz.q: D and E are the midpoints of AB and AC in ΔABC, and BC = 14 cm. What is DE?
quiz.explain: The segment joining the midpoints of two sides is parallel to the third side and half of it: 14 ÷ 2 = 7 cm.
quiz.mistake: Thinks DE equals BC because they are parallel

quiz.q: By what other name is the Basic Proportionality Theorem known?
quiz.explain: It is named after the Greek mathematician Thales.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the names of famous theorems

quiz.q: ABCD is a trapezium with AB ∥ DC, and its diagonals meet at O. Which ratio equals AO/OC?
quiz.explain: Draw a line through O parallel to AB and DC and apply BPT in two triangles. This shows the diagonals cut each other in the same ratio: AO/OC = BO/OD.
quiz.mistake: Writes the second ratio upside down

teach.ask: Gappu draws a line across a triangle: 'When does this line cut the sides in the same ratio?'
teach.praise: Chirp! Parallel to one side means the other two sides are cut in the same ratio. Thales says hi!
teach.nudge: What must be true about the line, and what happens to the two sides it cuts?

learn.hook: You don't need to check all six parts — just the right three clues prove two triangles are similar!
points: AAA (or AA) criterion: if two angles of one triangle equal two angles of another, the triangles are similar (the third angles are then equal too).
SSS criterion: if all three pairs of corresponding sides are in the same ratio, the triangles are similar.
SAS criterion: if one angle is equal and the sides including that angle are in the same ratio, the triangles are similar.
For triangles, equal angles guarantee proportional sides and proportional sides guarantee equal angles.
SSA is NOT a similarity criterion. Always write the vertices in the matching order.

example.q: A girl 1.5 m tall casts a 2 m shadow. At the same time a pole casts a 12 m shadow. How tall is the pole?
steps: The sun's rays make the same angle with the ground, and both stand at 90°, so the triangles are similar (AA)

learn.reallife: Surveyors find the height of a temple tower or a tall tree using a stick and shadows — no climbing needed!

games.title: Name the criterion

One equal angle with the sides around it in the same ratio

games.title: Similar or not?
items: If two angles of one triangle equal two angles of another, the triangles are similar.
The third angles must also match, since each triangle's angles add to 180°.
SSA is a similarity criterion.
Two sides and a non-included angle do not fix the shape.
Triangles with sides 3, 4, 5 and 6, 8, 10 are similar.
Each ratio is 2, so they are similar by SSS.
Triangles with sides 2, 3, 4 and 4, 6, 9 are similar.
If ΔABC ~ ΔDEF, then AB/DE = BC/EF = CA/FD.
Corresponding sides follow the order of the letters.
Two triangles with one pair of equal angles are always similar.
One equal angle is not enough; you need two.

quiz.q: Two triangles have sides 4, 6, 8 cm and 6, 9, 12 cm. Are they similar, and by which criterion?
quiz.explain: 6/4 = 9/6 = 12/8 = 1.5. All three sides are in the same ratio, so the triangles are similar by SSS.
quiz.mistake: Thinks sides must be equal, not just proportional

quiz.q: Meena, 1.5 m tall, casts a 2.5 m shadow. At the same time a tower casts a 40 m shadow. How tall is the tower?
quiz.explain: The triangles are similar (AA), so height/shadow is equal: 1.5/2.5 = h/40, giving h = 24 m.
quiz.mistake: Uses shadow/height on one side and height/shadow on the other

quiz.q: In ΔABC and ΔPQR, ∠A = ∠P = 40° and AB/PQ = AC/PR = 2/3. By which criterion are they similar?
quiz.explain: An equal angle (∠A = ∠P) with the sides including it in the same ratio is the SAS criterion.
quiz.mistake: Calls it SSS without having the third pair of sides

quiz.q: In ΔABC, ∠A = 65° and ∠B = 45°. In ΔDEF, ∠D = 65° and ∠F = 70°. Are the two triangles similar, and with which vertex order?
options: Only if the sides are equal
quiz.mistake: Writes the vertices in the wrong matching order

quiz.q: ΔABC ~ ΔPQR, with AB = 3 cm, BC = 4 cm, CA = 5 cm and PQ = 6 cm. What is the perimeter of ΔPQR?
quiz.explain: The scale factor is 6/3 = 2, so the perimeter is 2 × (3 + 4 + 5) = 24 cm.
quiz.mistake: Gives the perimeter of ΔABC

quiz.q: In ΔABC, DE ∥ BC with D on AB and E on AC. AD = 2 cm, AB = 6 cm and DE = 3 cm. What is BC?
quiz.explain: ΔADE ~ ΔABC by AA (corresponding angles are equal). So DE/BC = AD/AB = 2/6, giving BC = 3 × 6 ÷ 2 = 9 cm.
quiz.mistake: Uses AD/DB = 2/4 instead of AD/AB

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT a criterion for similarity of triangles?
quiz.explain: Two sides and an angle that is not between them do not fix the shape of a triangle.
quiz.mistake: Assumes any three parts are enough

quiz.q: In right ΔABC with ∠B = 90°, BD is drawn perpendicular to AC. Which triangle is ΔADB similar to?
quiz.explain: In ΔADB and ΔABC, ∠A is common and ∠ADB = ∠ABC = 90°. By AA, A ↔ A, D ↔ B, B ↔ C, so ΔADB ~ ΔABC.
quiz.mistake: Gets the order of the matching vertices wrong

teach.ask: Gappu has two triangles: 'Do I have to measure everything to know they are similar?'
teach.praise: Tweet tweet! AA, SSS or SAS — any one of these clues is enough. Detective Gappu is ready!
teach.nudge: What are the three shortcuts, and do sides need to be equal or just in the same ratio?

learn.hook: Pythagoras goes to the graph paper: find the distance between any two points without a ruler!
points: The distance between P(x₁, y₁) and Q(x₂, y₂) is PQ = √[(x₂ − x₁)² + (y₂ − y₁)²].
It comes from Pythagoras theorem: the horizontal gap and the vertical gap are the two shorter sides of a right triangle.
The distance of P(x, y) from the origin O(0, 0) is √(x² + y²).
The order of the points does not matter, because the differences are squared.
If the points are on the same horizontal or vertical line, the distance is just the difference of the changing coordinate.

example.q: Find the distance between A(−2, 3) and B(4, −5).

learn.reallife: Map apps work out straight-line distances between places using coordinates, just like this formula.

quiz.mistake: Adds the gaps (8 + 6 = 14) instead of using squares

quiz.q: How far is the point (−5, 12) from the origin?

quiz.q: What is the distance between (a, 0) and (0, a), where a > 0?
quiz.mistake: Adds the two gaps and gets 2a

quiz.q: The points (1, k) and (4, 5) are 5 units apart. What can k be?
quiz.explain: 3² + (5 − k)² = 25 gives (5 − k)² = 16, so 5 − k = ±4 and k = 1 or 9.
quiz.mistake: Takes only the positive square root

quiz.q: On a town map, Riya's house is at (2, 1) and her school at (8, 9), where 1 unit = 100 m. How far apart are they in a straight line?
quiz.explain: Distance = √(6² + 8²) = 10 units, and 10 × 100 m = 1000 m.
quiz.mistake: Forgets to use the map scale, or adds 6 + 8

quiz.q: What is the distance between (−6, 2) and (−2, −1)?
quiz.explain: Δx = −2 − (−6) = 4 and Δy = −1 − 2 = −3, so the distance is √(16 + 9) = 5.
quiz.mistake: Forgets to take the square root (25) or mishandles the negative signs

quiz.q: What is the distance of the point (x, y) from the origin?
quiz.explain: Use the distance formula with (0, 0): √[(x − 0)² + (y − 0)²] = √(x² + y²).
quiz.mistake: Forgets the square root, or adds the coordinates

quiz.q: Which point is nearest to the origin?
quiz.mistake: Ignores negative coordinates or just adds the coordinates

teach.praise: Chirp! Subtract, square, add and take the square root. We are 5 units apart!

topics.title: Using distances: shapes and collinear points

learn.hook: With just the distance formula you can prove points are in a straight line, or spot a hidden square!
points: Points A, B, C are collinear (on one line) if the two shorter distances add up to the longest, e.g. AB + BC = AC.
Isosceles triangle: two sides equal. Equilateral: all three sides equal.
Right triangle: the square of the longest side equals the sum of the squares of the other two (converse of Pythagoras).
Quadrilaterals: four equal sides and equal diagonals → square; four equal sides only → rhombus; opposite sides equal and equal diagonals → rectangle.
To find a point equidistant from A and B, set PA² = PB² (squares avoid messy roots).

example.q: Show that A(1, 1), B(4, 5) and C(7, 9) are collinear.
steps: AB + BC = 5 + 5 = 10 = AC, so the points lie on one line
example.answer: A, B and C are collinear

learn.reallife: Planners check whether three bus stops lie on one straight road, or whether a plot of land is a perfect square, using coordinates.

games.title: Shape spotter
items: If AB + BC = AC, then A, B and C are collinear.
B lies on the segment AC, so all three are on one line.
A quadrilateral with four equal sides is always a square.
It could be a rhombus with no right angle; the diagonals must also be equal for a square.
The points (0, 0), (3, 0) and (0, 4) form a right triangle.
The sides are 3, 4 and 5, and 3² + 4² = 5².
The points (0, 0), (2, 0) and (1, √3) form an equilateral triangle.
Each side is 2: for example √(1² + (√3)²) = √4 = 2.
The points (1, 2), (2, 3) and (4, 6) are collinear.
√2 + √13 ≈ 5.02, which is not equal to the longest distance 5.
The point (3, 3) is equidistant from (0, 0) and (6, 0).
Both distances are √18.

quiz.q: Are the points A(1, 5), B(2, 3) and C(−2, 11) collinear?
options: No, because no two distances are equal
Yes, because all distances are equal
No, because they form a right triangle
quiz.explain: AB = √5, AC = √45 = 3√5 and BC = √80 = 4√5. Since √5 + 3√5 = 4√5, AB + AC = BC, so the points are collinear.

quiz.q: What kind of triangle has vertices A(0, 0), B(4, 0) and C(4, 3)?
quiz.explain: AB = 4, BC = 3 and AC = 5. Since 3² + 4² = 5², the angle at B is 90°.
quiz.mistake: Does not test the Pythagoras condition

quiz.q: Which point on the y-axis is equidistant from (2, 3) and (−4, 1)?
quiz.explain: Let P = (0, y). 4 + (y − 3)² = 16 + (y − 1)² gives −6y + 13 = −2y + 17, so y = −1. Both distances are √20.
quiz.mistake: Takes a point on the x-axis instead of the y-axis

quiz.q: What figure do the points (1, 1), (4, 1), (4, 4) and (1, 4) form?

A rectangle that is not a square

quiz.q: P(x, 3) is equidistant from A(1, 1) and B(5, 1). What is x?
quiz.mistake: Makes an error expanding the squares

quiz.q: A circle has centre (2, −1) and passes through (5, 3). What is its radius?
quiz.explain: The radius is the distance from the centre to the point: √(3² + 4²) = √25 = 5.
quiz.mistake: Forgets to take the square root, or adds the gaps

quiz.q: What kind of triangle has vertices (0, 0), (6, 0) and (3, 4)?
quiz.explain: The sides are 6, √(9 + 16) = 5 and √(9 + 16) = 5. Two equal sides make it isosceles; 5² + 5² ≠ 6², so it is not right-angled.
quiz.mistake: Assumes a triangle with whole-number sides is right-angled

quiz.q: Three laddoo stalls at a mela are at (3, 1), (6, 4) and (8, 6). Are they in a straight line?
options: No, because the first two gaps are unequal
Yes, because they are in the same row
quiz.explain: AB = √18 = 3√2, BC = √8 = 2√2 and AC = √50 = 5√2. Since 3√2 + 2√2 = 5√2, the stalls are collinear.
quiz.mistake: Thinks collinear points must be equally spaced

learn.hook: Want the exact spot one-third of the way from your home to school? The section formula pins it down!
points: The point P that divides the segment from A(x₁, y₁) to B(x₂, y₂) internally in the ratio m₁ : m₂ is P = ((m₁x₂ + m₂x₁)/(m₁ + m₂), (m₁y₂ + m₂y₁)/(m₁ + m₂)).
Remember: m₁ goes with the far end B, and m₂ with the near end A.
Midpoint (ratio 1 : 1): ((x₁ + x₂)/2, (y₁ + y₂)/2).
To find an unknown ratio, call it k : 1 and solve for k.
Points of trisection divide a segment in the ratios 1 : 2 and 2 : 1.

example.q: Find the point that divides the join of A(−2, 5) and B(8, −5) in the ratio 2 : 3.

learn.reallife: Placing a water tank at a fair point between two villages, or a fielder between two cricket players, uses the section formula idea.

quiz.q: Kabir walks in a straight line from the gate G(2, 1) to a tree T(10, 5) and stops three-quarters of the way. Where is he?
quiz.explain: Three-quarters of the way means the ratio 3 : 1 from G. x = (3 × 10 + 1 × 2)/4 = 8 and y = (3 × 5 + 1 × 1)/4 = 4.
quiz.mistake: Uses the ratio 1 : 3, which is only a quarter of the way

teach.ask: Gappu wants to sit one-third of the way from his nest to the mango tree: 'How do I find that point?'
teach.praise: Chirp! Multiply by the ratio parts crosswise and divide by their sum. Found my spot!
teach.nudge: Which ratio number goes with which end point, and what do I divide by?

learn.hook: Three sides, one angle, six magic ratios — trigonometry is the secret language of right triangles!
points: In right ΔABC with ∠B = 90°, for the acute angle A: the side opposite A is BC, the side adjacent to A is AB, and AC is the hypotenuse.
sin A = opposite/hypotenuse, cos A = adjacent/hypotenuse, tan A = opposite/adjacent.
The reciprocals are cosec A = 1/sin A, sec A = 1/cos A and cot A = 1/tan A. Also tan A = sin A/cos A.
The ratios depend only on the angle, not on the size of the triangle.
For an acute angle, sin A and cos A are always less than 1, because the hypotenuse is the longest side. tan A can be any positive number.

example.q: If sin A = 3/5 for an acute angle A, find cos A and tan A.

learn.reallife: Ramp builders and roof makers use tan to set the right slope, so wheelchairs and rainwater both roll down safely.

games.title: Ratio reality check
items: sin A can be equal to 4/3 for an acute angle A.
sin A = opposite/hypotenuse, and the hypotenuse is the longest side, so sin A < 1.
tan A can be greater than 1.
tan A = opposite/adjacent, and the opposite side can be longer than the adjacent side.
cos A is short for cosecant A.
cos A is cosine A. Cosecant is written cosec A.
If a right triangle is enlarged to double size, sin A stays the same.
Both sides double, so their ratio does not change.
sec A = 1/cos A.
Secant is the reciprocal of cosine.
sin A means sin multiplied by A.
sin A is one symbol: the sine of the angle A.

quiz.q: In right ΔPQR, ∠Q = 90°, PQ = 5, QR = 12 and PR = 13. What is sin R?
quiz.explain: For ∠R, the opposite side is PQ = 5 and the hypotenuse is PR = 13. sin R = 5/13.
quiz.mistake: Uses the side next to R instead of the side opposite it

quiz.q: If tan A = 8/15, what is sin A?
quiz.explain: Take opposite = 8, adjacent = 15. Hypotenuse = √(64 + 225) = 17. sin A = 8/17.
quiz.mistake: Uses the adjacent side instead of the opposite side

quiz.q: If cos θ = 0.6, what is sec θ?
quiz.mistake: Thinks sec θ equals sin θ (4/5)

quiz.q: Which value can sin A NOT take for an acute angle A?
quiz.explain: sin A = opposite/hypotenuse, and the hypotenuse is the longest side, so sin A cannot be more than 1.
quiz.mistake: Forgets that the hypotenuse is the longest side

quiz.q: In ΔABC, right-angled at B, AB = 24 cm and BC = 7 cm. What is cos A?
quiz.explain: AC = √(576 + 49) = 25. For ∠A, adjacent = AB = 24, so cos A = 24/25.
quiz.mistake: Uses the opposite side BC instead of the adjacent side

quiz.q: If 3 cot A = 4, what is tan A?
quiz.explain: cot A = 4/3, and tan A = 1/cot A = 3/4.
quiz.mistake: Thinks tan A and cot A are equal

quiz.q: A 5 m ladder leans against a wall with its foot 3 m from the wall. What is the cosine of the angle it makes with the ground?
quiz.explain: For the angle at the ground, the adjacent side is 3 m and the hypotenuse (the ladder) is 5 m. cos = 3/5.
quiz.mistake: Uses the height on the wall (4 m) instead of the distance on the ground

quiz.q: Kabir says sin 30° is bigger in a big triangle than in a small one. Is he right?
options: No, trigonometric ratios depend only on the angle
Yes, bigger triangles have bigger ratios
Yes, because the hypotenuse is longer
No, sin 30° is smaller in a big triangle
quiz.explain: Right triangles with the same acute angle are similar, so their sides are in the same ratio. sin 30° is always 1/2.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the ratio depends on the length of the sides

teach.ask: Gappu points at a right triangle: 'What do sin, cos and tan actually mean?'
teach.praise: Tweet! Opposite over hypotenuse, adjacent over hypotenuse, opposite over adjacent. SOH-CAH-TOA!
teach.nudge: Which sides of the triangle do I divide for sin, for cos and for tan?

learn.hook: Five special angles — 0°, 30°, 45°, 60° and 90° — have values every board exam expects you to know by heart!
points: cos runs the other way: cos 0° = 1, cos 30° = √3/2, cos 45° = 1/√2, cos 60° = 1/2, cos 90° = 0.
tan 0° = 0, tan 30° = 1/√3, tan 45° = 1, tan 60° = √3, and tan 90° is not defined.
These come from an equilateral triangle (for 30° and 60°) and an isosceles right triangle (for 45°).
As A increases from 0° to 90°, sin A increases from 0 to 1 and cos A decreases from 1 to 0.

example.q: Evaluate sin 60° cos 30° + sin 30° cos 60°.

learn.reallife: Set squares in your geometry box have angles 30°, 45°, 60° and 90° — exactly the standard angles!

quiz.q: If sin A = 1/2 and A is acute, what is A?

quiz.mistake: Gives B (30°) instead of A

quiz.q: Which of these is not defined?
quiz.explain: tan 90° = sin 90°/cos 90° = 1/0, and division by zero is not defined.
quiz.mistake: Thinks cos 90° = 0 means it is undefined

quiz.q: What is (1 − tan² 45°)/(1 + tan² 45°)?
quiz.mistake: Uses tan 45° = 0 by mistake

quiz.q: As angle A increases from 0° to 90°, what happens to cos A?
quiz.explain: cos 0° = 1 and cos 90° = 0, and cos A falls steadily in between.
quiz.mistake: Confuses the behaviour of cos A with sin A

quiz.q: In ΔABC, right-angled at B, ∠A = 30° and AC = 10 cm. What is BC?
quiz.explain: BC is opposite ∠A, so sin 30° = BC/AC. BC = 10 × 1/2 = 5 cm.
quiz.mistake: Uses cos 30° and gets 5√3 cm, which is AB

teach.ask: Gappu forgot his table: 'How can I remember sin of 0°, 30°, 45°, 60° and 90°?'
teach.praise: Chirp chirp! sin goes 0, 1/2, 1/√2, √3/2, 1 — and cos is the same list backwards!
teach.nudge: What is sin 30°, and what are the values at 0° and 90°?

learn.hook: Some trig equations are true for EVERY angle — these identities are your shortcuts for proofs!
points: sin²A + cos²A = 1 for every angle A from 0° to 90°. It comes from Pythagoras: divide (opp² + adj² = hyp²) by hyp².
Divide by cos²A: 1 + tan²A = sec²A (for 0° ≤ A < 90°).
Divide by sin²A: 1 + cot²A = cosec²A (for 0° < A ≤ 90°).
Use them to find all the other ratios when one ratio is known.
To prove an identity, start from the harder side and simplify it into the other side.

example.q: If sin A = 5/13 and A is acute, find sec A.
steps: cos A = 12/13 (A is acute, so positive)

learn.reallife: Sound engineers and phone signal designers rely on sin² + cos² = 1 when they mix and split waves.

games.title: Identity or impostor?
items: sin²A + cos²A = 1 for every angle A from 0° to 90°.
It follows from Pythagoras theorem.
sec²A − tan²A = 1.
Rearrange 1 + tan²A = sec²A.
sin A + cos A = 1 for every angle A.
At 45°, sin A + cos A = 2/√2 = √2, which is not 1.
1 + cot²A = sec²A.
The correct identity is 1 + cot²A = cosec²A.
(sec A − tan A)(sec A + tan A) = 1.
It equals sec²A − tan²A = 1.
tan²A − sec²A = 1.
tan²A − sec²A = −1.

quiz.q: Simplify (1 + tan²A) cos²A.
quiz.explain: 1 + tan²A = sec²A, and sec²A × cos²A = 1.
quiz.mistake: Multiplies only the 1 by cos²A

quiz.q: If cos A = 8/17 and A is acute, what is sin A?
quiz.mistake: Subtracts without squaring: 17 − 8 = 9

quiz.q: What is 9 sec²A − 9 tan²A?
quiz.explain: 9(sec²A − tan²A) = 9 × 1 = 9.
quiz.mistake: Forgets the factor 9 and writes 1

quiz.q: If sec θ + tan θ = 4, what is sec θ − tan θ?
quiz.explain: (sec θ + tan θ)(sec θ − tan θ) = sec²θ − tan²θ = 1, so sec θ − tan θ = 1/4.
steps: (sec θ + tan θ)(sec θ − tan θ) = 1
quiz.mistake: Thinks the two expressions are equal or just opposite in sign

quiz.q: If sin A = 7/25 and A is acute, what is tan A?
quiz.mistake: Writes tan A = cos A/sin A (24/7)

quiz.q: Simplify (1 + cot²A) sin²A.
quiz.explain: 1 + cot²A = cosec²A, and cosec²A × sin²A = 1.
quiz.mistake: Uses 1 + cot²A = sec²A by mistake

quiz.q: Which expression is equal to cos²A?
quiz.explain: From sin²A + cos²A = 1, cos²A = 1 − sin²A.
quiz.mistake: Gets the sign the wrong way round when rearranging

quiz.q: What is sin² 30° + cos² 30°?
quiz.explain: (1/2)² + (√3/2)² = 1/4 + 3/4 = 1, as the identity promises.
quiz.mistake: Forgets to square the values

teach.ask: Gappu heard sin²A + cos²A = 1 works for every angle: 'Why is that true?'
teach.praise: Tweet! Pythagoras divided by hypotenuse squared — so sin² plus cos² is always 1. Mind blown!
teach.nudge: Which famous theorem about right triangles is hiding inside this identity?

learn.hook: Look up at a kite or down from a balcony — the angle your eyes turn through is the key to measuring things you can't reach!
points: The line of sight is the straight line from your eye to the object you are looking at.
Angle of elevation: the angle between the horizontal and the line of sight when you look UP at an object.
Angle of depression: the angle between the horizontal and the line of sight when you look DOWN at an object.
The angle of elevation of A from B equals the angle of depression of B from A — they are alternate angles between parallel horizontal lines.
As you walk towards a tower, the angle of elevation of its top increases. If the height equals the distance, the angle is 45°.

example.q: A kite is flying on a 100 m string that makes an angle of 30° with the ground. How high is the kite? (Assume the string is straight.)
steps: The string is the hypotenuse; the height is opposite the 30° angle

learn.reallife: During Makar Sankranti, kite flyers can estimate how high their kite is from the string length and the angle it makes with the ground.

games.title: Line-of-sight check
items: The angle of elevation is measured from the horizontal.
It is the angle between the horizontal line and the line of sight.
The angle of depression of a point P from the top of a tower equals the angle of elevation of the top from P.
They are alternate angles between parallel horizontal lines.
As you walk towards a tower, the angle of elevation of its top decreases.
It increases — the top looks steeper as you get closer.
If a tower's height equals your distance from its foot, the angle of elevation is 45°.
tan θ = height/distance = 1, so θ = 45°.
The angle of depression is measured from the vertical line.
It is measured down from the horizontal line.
A longer shadow of the same pole means the sun is lower in the sky.
A smaller angle of elevation of the sun gives a longer shadow.

quiz.q: A tower's height equals the distance of a point from its foot. What is the angle of elevation of the top from that point?
quiz.explain: tan θ = height/distance = 1, so θ = 45°.
quiz.mistake: Thinks equal sides give 60° as in an equilateral triangle

quiz.q: A kite flies on a 60 m string at an angle of elevation of 30°. How high is it?
quiz.explain: sin 30° = height/60, so height = 60 × 1/2 = 30 m.
quiz.mistake: Uses cos 30° and gets 30√3 m

quiz.q: A 10 m pole casts a shadow 10√3 m long. What is the sun's angle of elevation?
quiz.mistake: Computes shadow/height and gets 60°

quiz.q: From the top of a 20 m building, the angle of depression of a scooter on the road is 45°. How far is the scooter from the building?
quiz.explain: The angle of elevation of the top from the scooter is also 45°. tan 45° = 20/d = 1, so d = 20 m.
quiz.mistake: Uses sin or cos instead of tan, or puts the distance on top of the fraction

quiz.q: Why is the angle of depression of B from A equal to the angle of elevation of A from B?
options: They are alternate angles between parallel horizontal lines
quiz.explain: The horizontal lines through A and B are parallel, and the line AB is a transversal, so the two angles are alternate angles.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up alternate and vertically opposite angles

quiz.q: The sun's angle of elevation rises from 30° to 60°. What happens to the shadow of a flagpole?
quiz.explain: shadow = height/tan θ. tan 60° is bigger than tan 30°, so the shadow gets shorter.
quiz.mistake: Thinks a higher sun makes a longer shadow

quiz.q: A 6 m ladder leans against a wall and reaches a height of 3√3 m. What angle does it make with the ground?
quiz.mistake: Uses cos instead of sin and gets 30°

quiz.q: Kabir's eyes are 1.6 m above the ground. He stands 18.4 m from a flagpole and sees its top at an angle of elevation of 45°. How tall is the flagpole?
quiz.explain: Above eye level the height is 18.4 × tan 45° = 18.4 m. Add his eye height: 18.4 + 1.6 = 20 m.
quiz.mistake: Forgets to add the height of Kabir's eyes

points: Draw a neat figure: the object is vertical, the ground is horizontal, so you get a right triangle.

Use sin θ = height/hypotenuse when you know a slanting length, like a ladder or a kite string.
If the observer's eye is above the ground, add the eye height to the height found from the triangle.
For two angles seen from two places, write one equation for each triangle and solve them together.

quiz.q: From a point 40 m from the foot of a water tower, the angle of elevation of its top is 30°. How tall is the tower?

quiz.q: A storm bends a tree so that its top touches the ground 6 m from the foot, making an angle of 30° with the ground. How tall was the tree?
quiz.explain: Standing part = 6 tan 30° = 2√3 m. Broken part = 6/cos 30° = 4√3 m. Total = 6√3 m (about 10.39 m).
quiz.mistake: Finds only the standing part (2√3 m) and forgets the broken part

quiz.q: A kite flies on an 80 m string at an angle of elevation of 60°. How high is the kite?

quiz.q: From a point 20 m from a building, the top of the building is at 45° elevation and the top of a flagpole on it is at 60°. How long is the flagpole?
quiz.explain: Building height = 20 tan 45° = 20 m. Height to flagpole top = 20 tan 60° = 20√3 m. Flagpole = 20√3 − 20 = 20(√3 − 1) m.
quiz.mistake: Gives the total height instead of subtracting the building

quiz.q: You know a ladder's length and the angle it makes with the ground. Which ratio gives the height it reaches?
quiz.explain: Height is opposite the angle and the ladder is the hypotenuse, so use sin θ = height/ladder.
quiz.mistake: Uses tan, which needs the ground distance instead

quiz.q: From the top of a 10 m building, the angle of elevation of a tower's top is 30°. From the building's foot it is 60°. How tall is the tower?

If you walk a known distance towards a tower, set up two triangles that share the same height.

steps: The angle of elevation of the top from the boat is also 30°
